name: Perm / texture perm

lead: A perm chemically reshapes hair into waves or curls, and texture perms use the same idea for volume and a wavy or curly look. The curl is visible at once and gives a fuller, more styled head of hair.

On looksmaxxing forums users describe it as a way to change facial framing, with some claiming a boost of about 1 PSL and a way to cover weaker eye-area features. No attractiveness studies of perms were found.

paras: A reducing agent such as thioglycolate breaks keratin disulfide bonds while hair is wrapped on rods, and a neutralizer, usually hydrogen peroxide, reforms them in the curled shape. Modern perms descend from the 1938 cold wave, and results grow out as new hair appears.
Chemical processing can irritate the scalp and damage hair, and related chemical relaxers are associated with burns, dermatitis, breakage and hair loss.

angle.text: Forum users get perms for added texture and volume, with posters describing a boost of about 1 PSL and a way to soften weaker eye-area features. The curl change is visible at once; no attractiveness research has tested the rating claims.

lead: A perm (permanent wave) is a chemical hairstyling procedure that reshapes hair into waves or curls by breaking and reforming the disulfide bonds in keratin. A reducing agent, classically ammonium thioglycolate, breaks the bonds while the hair is wrapped on rods, and a neutralizer such as hydrogen peroxide reforms them in the new shape.[1]

Modern perms descend from the 1938 cold wave, which required no heat, after earlier thermal and electric methods in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; types now include alkaline, acid, exothermic and digital perms.[1] A texture perm refers to the use of such methods to add wave or curl for volume and texture.

On looksmaxxing forums, perms are discussed as a hair-based way to change facial framing; users there have claimed that a perm adds a point on the PSL scale.[2][3] No published clinical studies of perms for attractiveness were found in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Thioglycolate reduction, peroxide neutralization of disulfide bonds[1]
Alkaline, acid, exothermic, digital, soft and spot perms[1]

paras: Hair's strength and elasticity come from disulfide bonds between keratin chains. In a perm, ammonium or sodium thioglycolate at a pH of about 8 to 9.5 breaks these bonds over roughly 15 to 30 minutes while the hair is wound, and a neutralizer then reforms them.[1] Acid perms use glyceryl monothioglycolate at lower pH with added heat and are described as gentler on hair.[1] Related chemistry without rods is used in permanent relaxers.[1]

Marcel Grateau introduced a thermal waving method in 1872. In 1905 Karl Nessler demonstrated an electric method using caustic soda and heat, which could damage hair and was slow. Sulfur-based reducing agents were added around 1930, and Arnold Willatt developed the cold wave in 1938. Home perm kits became popular after World War II, and digital perms appeared in the 21st century.[1]

Wikipedia's perm article does not provide a dedicated risk section; it notes that early heat-based methods could burn hair and scalp and carried shock or scalding hazards.[1] Chemical relaxers using related chemistry are associated with scalp burns, dermatitis, breakage and hair loss in Wikipedia's relaxer article.[4]
